summary: This Allucent article explains how sponsors should prepare an Initial Pediatric Study Plan (iPSP) under the FDA's pediatric rules. It traces the history of pediatric labeling regulation from the 1990s through PREA in 2003, then covers iPSP timing, orphan designation exemptions, extrapolation of adult efficacy, waivers and deferrals, pediatric formulations, and amendments. It closes by stressing that an agreed iPSP is critical for a successful marketing filing.
one_line: Guide to preparing FDA Initial Pediatric Study Plans (iPSPs), covering PREA requirements, timelines, orphan exemptions, extrapolation, waivers and amendments.
key_facts: The Food and Drug Administration began increasing efforts to ensure pediatric use information was provided in all drug labels in 1994.
The Pediatric Rule of 1998 was overturned in 2002 after legal battles.
Congress granted the FDA authority to regulate pediatric studies with the Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) in 2003.
Additional iPSP requirements implemented in 2012 require Sponsors to include a proposed timeline and planned design of pediatric studies during the IND stage.
The submission of an iPSP should occur no later than 60 days following the end of phase 2 (EOP2) meeting.
The total review period with the FDA for an iPSP is 210 days.
When considering timelines, the article advises budgeting at least two months to draft an iPSP.
Orphan designation applies to drugs or biologics intended for a disease or condition that affects less than 200,000 people in the United States.
The RACE for Children Act was incorporated as Title V of the 2017 FDA Reauthorization Act (FDARA) on August 18, 2017, to amend PREA.

Under the RACE for Children Act, new drugs intended for adult cancers and directed at a molecular target substantially relevant to pediatric cancer must conduct pediatric studies regardless of orphan status; this applies to applications with planned submission dates after August 18, 2020.
In almost all cases, safety cannot be extrapolated from adults, but safety data can be leveraged, particularly if the mechanism is well known and there is an exposure-response relationship.
The pediatric dose is typically determined based on modeling and simulation.
FDA formally grants waivers and deferrals when it issues an approval letter for the marketing application, not with the response to the iPSP.

Requests for waivers can be made if necessary studies are impossible or highly impracticable, or if the drug does not represent a meaningful therapeutic benefit over existing therapies for pediatric patients.
Failure to include an agreed iPSP in a marketing application subject to PREA may be grounds for a refuse-to-file action.
Changing a date in Section 11 that would significantly delay pediatric studies by more than 12 months is an example of an amendment to a PSP.

entities.name: Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
entities.role: US regulator that increased efforts from 1994 to require pediatric use information in drug labels and reviews iPSPs

entities.name: Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA)
entities.role: 2003 law granting the FDA authority to regulate pediatric studies, under which Sponsors must assess safety and effectiveness in pediatric populations

entities.name: FDA Modernization Act of 1997
entities.role: Act that implemented additional incentives and requirements for conducting pediatric studies

entities.name: Pediatric Rule of 1998
entities.role: Rule that implemented additional requirements for pediatric studies and was overturned in 2002 after legal battles

entities.name: RACE for Children Act
entities.role: Act incorporated as Title V of the 2017 FDA Reauthorization Act (FDARA) to amend PREA, requiring pediatric studies for certain adult cancer drugs

entities.name: 2017 FDA Reauthorization Act (FDARA)
entities.role: Legislation in which the RACE for Children Act was incorporated as Title V

entities.name: Initial pediatric study plan (iPSP)
entities.role: Proposed plan containing timeline and planned design of pediatric studies, required for NDA or BLA marketing applications

entities.name: Pediatric Oncology Program
entities.role: FDA program that released a Pediatric Molecular Target List to help determine whether drugs are affected by the RACE for Children Act

entities.name: Allucent
entities.role: Company whose website hosts the article and which invites readers to contact it for help with iPSP needs

entities.name: Pediatric Molecular Target List
entities.role: FDA list differentiating targets based on their relevance to growth or progression of pediatric cancers
